meta.title: Río Santiago / Lerma–Chapala–Santiago pollution around Guadalajara – research dataset
notes: RETC data: SEMARNAT RETC bulk file RETC_2004-2022.zip (federal-jurisdiction establishments only; state-jurisdiction facilities and non-reporters are absent). "to_water" = AGUA column (direct release to water bodies); "to_sewer" = ALCANTARILLADO (transfer to municipal sewer). Many RETC metal quantities are self-reported estimates (often flow × NOM limit) and include obvious outliers; treat single-year spikes as unverified.
Coordinates labelled "RETC" are the facility's self-reported lat/lon (degrees-minutes-seconds converted to decimal); some filings are rounded or inconsistent between years — see coord_source_detail.

Greenpeace "Ríos tóxicos" (2012) is a poster/infographic without company names; the company list comes from the companion 2012 Greenpeace/UCCS/Un Salto de Vida study "Estudio de la contaminación en la cuenca del río Santiago y la salud pública en la región".
The CNDH recommendation about the 2008 death of Miguel Ángel López Rocha is No. 12/2010 (issued 2 Mar 2010), not 12/2009. The 2022 CNDH recommendation is 134/2022.

The IMTA 2011 study (chapter IX on the riosantiago.jalisco.gob.mx site) lists ~26 industrial discharges sampled in 2009-2010 (many are pig farms in Los Altos); it does not give coordinates. The figure of ~280 discharges is CONAGUA's count cited by CNDH 134/2022.
CONAGUA RENAMECA open data provide DBO5, DQO, SST, coliforms, E. coli, DO and toxicity plus semáforo, but not heavy metals.

municipal_discharges.name: PTAR Agua Prieta (Zapopan)
municipal_discharges.operator: Concession: Atlatec / Renova Atlatec (RETC 2020-2022); formerly "Tratadora de Aguas de Zapopan" (RETC 2014-2019); CEA Jalisco
known_issues: Designed for NOM-001-SEMARNAT-1996 (Type B receiving body); Jalisco planning sheet says it requires modernization (≈MXN 678 M) to comply with NOM-001-SEMARNAT-2021; potential annual discharge-fee liability ≈MXN 958.5 M if non-compliant.

Self-reported RETC releases to water by the operator are the largest in the region (e.g., 2022: ≈17.1 t Ni, ≈11.6 t Cr, ≈12.1 t Pb, ≈1.3 t Cd, ≈130 kg Hg) — these are loads passing through the plant, likely estimated from flow × concentration.
CEA/FONNOR 2022 diagnostic found cadmium 0.027 mg/L at station E16 (Río Santiago, Ixtlahuacán del Río) and inferred Agua Prieta discharges as the nearest source.
Northwest AMG discharges (San Andrés, San Gaspar, Osorio) and the Río Blanco PTAR expansion were still pending federal funding as of 2024.

municipal_discharges.name: PTAR El Ahogado (Tlajomulco de Zúñiga, next to Presa El Ahogado)
municipal_discharges.operator: Concession: Aguas Tratadas de Guadalajara (RETC 2014-2021) / Mitsui & Co. Infrastructure Solutions (RETC 2022); CEA Jalisco
municipal_discharges.capacity_note: RRS2050 (2024): a 1,000 L/s module was added "for a total of 3,250 L/s". The 2,250 L/s original figure is inferred (3,250 − 1,000), not directly quoted.
municipal_discharges.receiving_water: Presa / Arroyo El Ahogado → Río Santiago above El Salto–Juanacatlán
known_issues: Greenpeace (Jan 2016 sampling) found nonylphenols, octylphenol, phthalates (DBP, DiBP, DEP, DMP), bisphenol-A, triphenyl phosphate and PFOA in the treated effluent, concluding the domestic-sewage plant receives industrial wastewater.
CNDH Rec. 134/2022: El Salto officials (Sept 2021) said the plant is over capacity and much wastewater bypasses it directly into Canal El Ahogado; CNDH staff observed strong odors at the outfall.
Operator RETC releases to water 2022: ≈8.8 t Ni, ≈7.6 t Cr, ≈7.6 t Pb, ≈0.76 t Cd, ≈227 kg Hg.

municipal_discharges.name: PTAR Río Blanco (SIAPA, Zapopan)
known_issues: Expansion of the Río Blanco PTAR was among works for which CONAGUA did not allocate budget under the 8 Oct 2020 collaboration agreement (RRS2050, 2024). Capacity not found in sources reviewed.

municipal_discharges.name: Untreated northwest AMG discharges: San Andrés, San Gaspar and Osorio (barranca del Río Santiago)
municipal_discharges.coord_precision: none – exact outfalls not located; they discharge into the Santiago canyon on the NE edge of Guadalajara/Tonalá
known_issues: Listed in RRS2050 (2024) as discharges still to be controlled; CONAGUA had not allocated the agreed budget. The state targets ~98% basin sanitation once these and Río Blanco are addressed.

municipal_discharges.name: El Salto municipality – 7 direct untreated discharges to the Río Santiago
municipal_discharges.coord_precision: municipal seat (INEGI 20°31'10"N 103°10'54"W) – NOT the discharge points
known_issues: CNDH Rec. 134/2022: El Salto officials (1 Sept 2021) reported 7 wastewater discharges directly to the Río Santiago without treatment or CONAGUA permit.

municipal_discharges.name: Poncitlán municipal sanitation systems
known_issues: CNDH Rec. 134/2022: of 6 sanitation systems only 1 operating, another at 20%, rest out of service (Sept 2021); CEA 2019 found abandonment and design defects.

municipal_discharges.name: Juanacatlán municipal PTARs
known_issues: CNDH Rec. 134/2022: 3 PTARs, one out of operation due to cable theft; electricity costs make operation onerous (Sept 2021).

municipal_discharges.name: Canal / Presa Las Pintas (south AMG sewage canal feeding El Ahogado)
municipal_discharges.coord_precision: CONAGUA RENAMECA site OCLSP3681M1 (Presa Las Pintas cortina)
known_issues: RENAMECA 2012-2025 aggregate: red semáforo (DQO, E. coli, fecal coliforms, low bottom DO).
CEA/FONNOR 2022: water toxicity (Daphnia CE50 48h) positive at Arroyo Las Pintas station E19.

Oct 2026: CEA reported 103 wastewater/industrial discharges found by CONAGUA inspectors; effluent reached the old Las Pintas system and, before gates closed, the Miravalle drinking-water plant intake.

facts.fact: Accelerated industrialization of the El Salto industrial corridor (El Salto, Juanacatlán, Poncitlán, Ocotlán), later extending to Tlajomulco and Ixtlahuacán de los Membrillos with NAFTA-era investment: chemical, petrochemical, metal-mechanic, textile, automotive, electronics, pharmaceutical and food plants.
PROFEPA registered 159 industries discharging wastewater to the Río Santiago (Ocotlán area and two corridors); CONAGUA counted 280 discharges, 266 of them into the Santiago.

IMTA study for CEA Jalisco (sampling Mar 2009–May 2010) detected 1,090 toxic substances, chemicals and metals in discharges and river water; 87–94% of industries failed at least one NOM-001-SEMARNAT-1996 parameter, and industrial discharges were more polluting than municipal ones.

Miguel Ángel López Rocha (8–9 years old) fell into the Río Santiago/El Ahogado canal at El Salto on 25 Jan 2008 and died on 13 Feb 2008; hospital notes diagnosed arsenic poisoning. CNDH Recommendation 12/2010 (2 Mar 2010) faulted CONAGUA for failing to enforce environmental norms.

An IMTA June 2008 monitoring report (cited by CNDH 12/2010) concluded the main source of Santiago pollution is water from Arroyo El Ahogado; Puente Grande showed significant acute toxicity attributed to heavy metals.
Jalisco human rights commission (CEDHJ) issued Macro-Recomendación 1/2009 with 100 points addressed to the governor, 14 municipalities, SIAPA and CEA.

Greenpeace/UCCS/Un Salto de Vida study: >90% of residents of El Salto, Juanacatlán and Ocotlán live within 5 km of the Santiago, El Ahogado or Zula; 51% (El Salto) and 81% (Juanacatlán) live within 1 km. Mortality from hypertensive kidney disease and renal failure rose in El Salto and Juanacatlán in 2007–2010.

The same study listed the 10 facilities with the highest RETC-reported heavy-metal and cyanide discharges (2004–2009): CIBA (now Huntsman), Grupo Celanese, Cervecería Modelo de Guadalajara, Nestlé México, Hilasal Mexicana, Cervecería Cuauhtémoc Moctezuma, Casa Cuervo, IBM de México, Servicios Estrella Azul de Occidente (only 9 names are printed).

A UASLP study commissioned by CEA (2009–2010) of ~300 children found high exposure to lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury, benzene and POPs in El Salto, Juanacatlán, La Cofradía and Puente Grande; results were kept secret for years. CEDHJ found rights violations by CEA and health authorities (June 2022).
At the El Salto–Juanacatlán waterfall the polluted, sulfate-rich water churns into thick foam that wind carries onto the bridge and homes; residents report headaches, nausea and eye irritation.
All urban drains flow into the El Salto–Juanacatlán diversion dam; foam bubbles 15–50 cm in diameter rise from the falls and drift onto passers-by and neighbours.

UN Working Group on Business and Human Rights members visited the falls in 2016 and called it "una catástrofe ecológica"; Greenpeace sampling the same year found nonylphenols, phthalates and bisphenol-A in treated effluent of PTAR El Ahogado.

PROFEPA Recommendation PFPA/1/2C.5/03/2017 to upstream Lerma states (Durango, Guanajuato, Edomex, Michoacán, Nayarit, Querétaro, Zacatecas): the Lerma–Santiago basin shows arsenic, cyanide, mercury, benzene, vinyl chloride, lead, cadmium, chromium and other contaminants — pollution also arrives from the Lerma via Lake Chapala.

IACHR granted precautionary measures MC-708-19 (Resolution 7/2020, 5 Feb 2020) to residents within ~5 km of the Santiago in Juanacatlán and El Salto and four Poncitlán localities on Lake Chapala (San Pedro Itzicán, Agua Caliente, Chalpicote, Mezcala).

CNDH Recommendation 134/2022 (30 Jun 2022) to SEMARNAT, CONAGUA, PROFEPA, the federal Health Ministry, Jalisco's governor and El Salto, Juanacatlán and Poncitlán: violations of rights to a healthy environment, water and sanitation, health and children's best interest.

Chronic kidney disease has been reported since the early 1990s on the Lake Chapala shore, with most cases in San Pedro Itzicán and Agua Caliente (Poncitlán); authorities attribute it to multiple factors and have not established a causal link to water pollution.

RENAMECA data reviewed by CNDH: Santiago water was "strongly contaminated" for fecal coliforms at all 9 study sites and "contaminated" for DQO at almost all; high Vibrio fischeri toxicity at the site before Nestlé (Ocotlán) and after Arroyo El Ahogado.

In CONAGUA's 2025 semáforo, every site with 2025 data on the Santiago from Ocotlán to Puente Grande, on Arroyo El Ahogado and on the Zula is RED (failing DQO and fecal coliforms/E. coli; Vibrio toxicity at El Ahogado sites); on the Lerma near Chapala 5 of 6 sites with 2025 data are red and one yellow.

The Santiago basin in Jalisco (6.29 M people) generates ~13,400 L/s of wastewater; 68 PTARs treat 9,926 L/s (74%), up from 7,764 L/s in 2018. Hydrogen sulfide at the El Salto–Juanacatlán dam fell from 10.82 to 9.10 mg/L after solar recirculators were installed.

CEA reported 103 wastewater and industrial discharges into the Río Santiago found by 40 CONAGUA inspectors; polluted water reached the Las Pintas system and the Miravalle water-treatment plant intake.

hotspots.name: Salto de Juanacatlán (El Salto–Juanacatlán falls and diversion dam)
hotspots.description: Once called the "Niagara of Mexico"; today the 20 m drop releases hydrogen sulfide and toxic foam over El Salto and Juanacatlán.

hotspots.name: Confluence of Arroyo El Ahogado with the Río Santiago
hotspots.coord_precision: CONAGUA station OCLSP3716M1 "Arroyo El Ahogado antes del Río Santiago" (approximate confluence)
hotspots.description: Point identified by CEA (Dec 2020) as the largest pollutant input to the Santiago; RENAMECA 2025: red, with Vibrio toxicity.

hotspots.name: Presa El Ahogado / PTAR El Ahogado / La Alameda
hotspots.coord_precision: approximate – PTAR El Ahogado OSM centroid; the dam is adjacent (CONAGUA lists a "Presa El Ahogado cortina" site at 20.56965,-103.25246 that could not be verified)
hotspots.description: Reservoir receiving sewage and industrial runoff of south Guadalajara and the El Salto industrial park; worst water quality in the 2012 Greenpeace/UNAM study; new housing (La Alameda) sits beside it.

hotspots.name: Puente camino a Penwalt (Arroyo El Ahogado)
hotspots.description: El Ahogado channel inside the El Salto industrial zone; RENAMECA 2025 red with DBO, DQO, Vibrio toxicity, E. coli failures.

hotspots.name: Puente Grande (Tonalá/Juanacatlán)
hotspots.description: Downstream of the falls; IMTA 2008 found significant acute toxicity attributed to heavy metals; UASLP 2009-2010 found high child exposure to metals here.

hotspots.name: Arcediano (Barranca de Huentitán)
hotspots.coord_precision: OpenStreetMap place node (Antiguo Pueblo de Arcediano)
hotspots.description: Site of the cancelled Arcediano dam meant to supply Guadalajara with Santiago water; the UASLP health study was linked to this project. RENAMECA Puente Arcediano: red.

hotspots.name: Río Santiago downstream of PTAR Agua Prieta (Paso de Guadalupe, Ixtlahuacán del Río)
hotspots.description: Cadmium 0.027 mg/L, ~7× the aquatic-life limit; second-highest priority point in the 2022 diagnostic.

hotspots.name: Ocotlán – Río Santiago source / Nestlé reach
hotspots.description: Where the Santiago leaves Lake Chapala and receives Ocotlán's industry and the Zula; red semáforo, high Vibrio toxicity reported 2012-2019.

hotspots.name: Río Zula at El Duque (Ocotlán)
hotspots.description: Zula tributary carrying Altos/tequila-district wastewater; 2025 fecal coliforms ≈660,000 NMP/100 mL, moderate Vibrio toxicity.

hotspots.name: Río Lerma mouth at Lake Chapala (La Barca–Jamay)
hotspots.description: The Lerma brings wastewater from Edomex, Querétaro, Guanajuato and Michoacán into Chapala, which feeds the Santiago; 2025 red (DQO, coliforms, SST).

hotspots.name: San Pedro Itzicán (Poncitlán, Lake Chapala shore)
hotspots.description: Community with high chronic kidney disease incidence; covered by IACHR MC-708-19.

hotspots.name: Agua Caliente (Poncitlán)
hotspots.coord_precision: not located – OSM "Agua Caliente" hamlet at 20.29430,-102.74681 is in Ocotlán municipality and may be a different place
hotspots.description: Lakeshore community with high CKD incidence; covered by MC-708-19.

hotspots.name: Mezcala (Poncitlán)
hotspots.description: Lakeshore community covered by IACHR MC-708-19.

hotspots.name: Relleno sanitario Los Laureles (Tonalá)
hotspots.description: Landfill next to the Santiago; CNDH 12/2010 found leachate pits without liner flowing toward the river; its closure is part of the state strategy.

hotspots.name: Presa Las Pintas (Tlaquepaque/El Salto)
hotspots.description: Sewage-laden reservoir on the Las Pintas canal that drains to El Ahogado; red semáforo, toxicity positive.
